text: Three lessons built up real pieces: a log destination, a small set of alerts, and the discipline to keep that alert set from turning into noise. Pulling them together into one checklist matters because it's easy to walk away thinking monitoring is done after setting a few things up, when some of those pieces were configured but never actually verified to work.

Five points, in order. Metrics configured — the environment's resources are confirmed reporting into the log destination from Lesson 13, not just technically eligible to. Alerts configured — the high-confidence set from Lesson 14 exists as real rules against real resources. Alerts tested — deliberately triggered once to confirm they actually fire. Notification configured — a real person is subscribed to the action group or SNS topic on the other end. And a dashboard created, showing the metrics that matter in one place.

The testing step is the one most worth calling out, because it's the easiest to skip. Temporarily forcing a threshold low enough to fire, confirming the notification actually arrives, and then restoring the real threshold is the only way to know an alert works end to end. An alert rule that's never actually fired is an assumption, not a confirmed working alert — syntactically valid is not the same thing as verified.

Walking all five points against the environment from Chapters 1 through 3 — metrics flowing, four alerts configured and test-fired, notifications confirmed, one dashboard showing it all — that's monitoring genuinely standing, not just assumed to be. But monitoring only tells you something went wrong. It doesn't get you back online, and a monitored environment with no backup still loses data permanently if a disk fails or something gets deleted by mistake.

That's a different problem with a different fix, and it's exactly where Chapter 5 picks up: Backup & Disaster Recovery Basics, starting with what RTO and RPO actually mean for a deployment like this one.
